1.e4 e5 2.Nc3.name: Vienna Game
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3.background: Named after the city of Vienna and popular in the nineteenth century, it began as a delayed King's Gambit. Weaver W. Adams famously claimed that it wins by force for White, whereas Nick de Firmian concludes in the 15th edition of Modern Chess Openings that it leads to equality with best play.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6.name: Vienna Game: Falkbeer Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6.background: Named after Ernst Falkbeer (1819–1885), the Austrian master and journalist who founded the Wiener Schachzeitung in 1855 and also gave his name to the Falkbeer Countergambit. It is the most common reply to the Vienna Game.
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and attacks e4, which the c3 knight must keep guarding. It also prepares to answer an attack on the centre with ...d5, striking back at once instead of defending. Taking a gambit pawn on f4 would be a mistake, since the push to e5 drives the knight back.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and defends e5. With no knight on f6 for a push to e5 to hit, Black can accept a gambit pawn on f4, which leads to very sharp play. Otherwise the set-up is solid and flexible, and White chooses between quiet development and attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bc5.name: Vienna Game: Anderssen Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bc5.background: An offbeat but playable alternative to the main replies; the former world champion José Raúl Capablanca played it as Black against Ilya Kan at Moscow 1936.
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bc5.strategy: Puts the bishop on the a7–g1 diagonal, where it eyes f2, and keeps Black's development flexible. It is offbeat but playable, and Black must watch e5: after Nf3, the natural ...Nc6 allows Nxe5 Nxe5 d4, forking bishop and knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4.strategy: Develops the bishop against the c3 knight, the guard of e4, and prepares ...Nf6. It is a playable sideline: a direct attack on g7 gains White nothing clear, and quieter play often transposes to other openings.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Defends e5 solidly and opens the c8 bishop, but restricts the f8 bishop to e7 and concedes space. The game often resembles a Philidor Defence, with White free to choose between quiet play and a sharper attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 f5.strategy: Strikes at e4 at once, but after 3.exf5 Black is a pawn down and the e8–h5 diagonal is open. Trying to regain the pawn with 3...d5 runs into 4.Qh5+.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Qe7.strategy: Defends e5, but the queen blocks the f8 bishop and stands exposed: 3.Nd5 attacks it and the c7 pawn at once, so the queen must move again.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Qf6.strategy: Eyes f2 but takes the f6 square from the g8 knight, and 3.Nd5 attacks the queen and the c7 pawn at once. The queen must move again while guarding c7, so Black has lost time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Qg5.strategy: Eyes g2, which the f1 bishop defends, but 3.d4 attacks the queen with the c1 bishop and the e5 pawn with the d-pawn. Black loses a tempo and has to give up the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Qh4.strategy: Attacks e4, which the c3 knight guards, and f2, which the king guards. 3.Nf3 hits the queen with a developing move and attacks e5 as well, so Black loses time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Be7.strategy: Develops the bishop modestly but blocks the queen and leaves e5 undefended against 3.Nf3. Black needs another move just to hold the pawn, and White gets a free hand in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bd6.strategy: Blocks the d-pawn and loses time after 3.Nb5, which attacks the bishop and c7. If Black ignores it, Nxd6+ cxd6 doubles the pawns and leaves White the two bishops.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where its only forward squares are b4 and c5 and it does nothing for e5. White develops and takes the centre against an undefended centre pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, blocks the h-pawn and leaves e5 undefended. After 3.d4 the c1 bishop eyes h6, and Bxh6 gxh6 would wreck the kingside pawns.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Ne7.strategy: Blocks the f8 bishop and the queen, leaves e5 undefended and puts no pressure on e4. White develops freely with 3.Nf3, attacking e5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that neither develops a piece nor contests the centre. After 3.Nf3 the e5 pawn is attacked and Black has to defend it a tempo down.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Advances the a-pawn for no purpose in the opening, loses a tempo and weakens b5. White develops with 3.Nf3, attacking e5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 against e4, but does nothing for e5, which 3.Nf3 attacks at once. The pawn move costs a tempo, and the bishop would only hit a well-guarded e4 pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 but leaves e5 without support and takes c6 from the b8 knight. After 3.Nf3 Black usually has to spend another tempo on defending e5, because 3...d5 4.exd5 cxd5 5.Nxe5 loses a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 c5.strategy: Leaves e5 undefended and weakens d5, a square the c3 knight can occupy at once. After 3.Nf3 Black needs to defend e5 anyway, so the c-pawn move has only cost time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 f6.strategy: Supports e5 but takes the f6 square from the g8 knight and weakens the king: with f7 empty, the a2–g8 and e8–h5 diagonals open for Bc4 and Qh5+. After 3.Bc4 the bishop already covers g8, so Black cannot castle short until the diagonal is closed.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 but ignores the centre and loosens the long diagonal. After 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 the queen attacks the h8 rook, and Black must block at once, since 4...Bg7? drops the bishop to 5.Qxg7.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Weakens the king's cover and the f5 and h5 squares and opens the long diagonal. After 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 the queen attacks the h8 rook, and blocking with 4...Nf6 shuts the d8 queen off from g5, so 5.Bxg5 wins a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: Loses a tempo on a pawn move that stops a bishop which cannot yet come to g5. e5 stays undefended, and White develops with 3.Nf3.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: A flank advance that weakens g5 and the kingside for no gain, with nothing done for development or against e4. 3.Nf3 attacks e5 immediately.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 too early: 3.exd5 wins a pawn, and 3...Qxd5 loses the queen to 4.Nxd5. After 3...Nf6 4.Bc4 the c3 knight and the bishop guard d5, so 4...Nxd5? 5.Nxd5 costs Black a piece.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Throws a pawn away: 3.Nxb5 or 3.Bxb5 wins it for nothing, since ...a6 only chases the piece back.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for good, blocks the f8 bishop and the queen and keeps the king in the centre, where 3.Nd5+ and a later f4 harass it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Ba3.strategy: Hangs the bishop to 3.bxa3: no Black piece guards a3, and there is no compensation for the piece.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4 3.Qg4.strategy: Goes for the undefended g7 pawn, and with it the rook on h8. It is a sharp, greedy try: Black can counterattack the queen at once, so White must be ready to run it around the board for a pawn while Black's pieces come out with tempo.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4 3.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once. The knight on c3 is pinned, but White does not mind: if Black takes on d4, the queen recaptures with threats on g7 and the bishop. White takes space and the initiative while Black's early bishop move has no follow-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop against f7 and calmly ignores Black's early bishop move. White keeps an easy lead in development and a flexible centre, and Black's bishop on b4 has little to bite on, since capturing on c3 hands White the pair of bishops.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4 3.Qg4 Nf6.name: Vienna Game: Zhuravlev Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4 3.Qg4 Nf6.strategy: Counters at once: the knight attacks the queen and the e4 pawn, and g7 is given up. If the queen takes it, the rook on g8 hits the queen and the g2 pawn comes under fire; Black is a pawn down but ahead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4 3.Qg4 Bf8.strategy: Retreats the bishop at once to cover g7, giving up the time spent on the sortie. Black is solid but passive, White's queen keeps its active post, and White gets a free hand in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bb4 3.Qg4 g6.strategy: Moves the g-pawn to g6, where f7 and h7 guard it, so the queen cannot take it. The cost is the dark squares around the king, and White's queen keeps its active post. A safe but slow answer that leaves Black behind in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bc5 3.Na4.name: Vienna Game: Hamppe-Meitner Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bc5 3.Na4.background: Named in honour of Carl Hamppe and Philipp Meitner, who played it in Vienna in 1872 in the game known as the Immortal Draw: Black sacrificed a bishop on f2, and White escaped with a draw by perpetual check.
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bc5 3.Na4.strategy: Attacks the bishop on c5, which nothing defends, aiming to win the bishop pair. But the knight is badly placed on the edge, and Black answers with the bishop sacrifice on f2: after Kxf2 Qh4+ the white king is dragged into a wild attack that favours Black.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bc5 3.Qg4.name: Vienna Game: Giraffe Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bc5 3.Qg4.strategy: Attacks g7 too early. Black hits the queen with a developing move and lets the pawn go: after Qxg7 Rg8 Qh6 Bxf2+ White's king is exposed, and Kxf2 loses the queen to a knight check on g4.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bc5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight with an attack on e5, the straightforward answer to Black's offbeat set-up. Black must defend the pawn at once and has no quick counterplay, so White keeps a small, lasting initiative with natural development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Bc5 3.f4.strategy: Strikes at e5 with the f-pawn, a King's Gambit with the queen's knight already developed. White accepts a looser king's side for central influence and the open f-file, and the knight on c3 guards e4, which gives the centre a firmer base than in the plain gambit.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4.name: Vienna Game: Omaha Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.f4.strategy: A King's Gambit with the knight already on c3: the f-pawn strikes at e5 and Black's d6 pawn already guards it. If Black takes, Black wins a pawn and can check on the weakened diagonal to the king.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.d4.strategy: Blows open the centre while Black's d6 pawn has shut in the king's bishop. If Black takes, White recaptures with the queen, which Black may harass with tempo, yet White keeps the more active development and more space. Black stays cramped and has to defend carefully.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops with an attack on e5, which d6 already guards. White keeps a flexible, solid set-up with the extra knight already out, and Black is left in a passive structure where the king's bishop is hemmed in. A quiet, sound way to play for a small edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 d6 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop to the active diagonal where it eyes f7, and keeps the centre closed. Black's solid pawns on e5 and d6 meet it without trouble, so White gets an ordinary, harmless development and no real pressure.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4.name: Vienna Game: Vienna Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4.background: Anthony Santasiere and Weaver W. Adams, among others, have advocated the gambit, but Raymond Keene wrote that it is considered too risky at the grandmaster level.
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4.strategy: Strikes at e5 at once, aiming to open the f-file and pull Black's e-pawn out of the centre. Taking on f4 is met by e5, driving the knight back, so Black has to answer in the centre. The price is a loosened king, with the e1-h4 diagonal open, in a sharp, open game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops with an eye on f7 and keeps the f-pawn at home, a calmer course than the gambit. The cost is that Black's knight can strike at e4 at once, so White must know the tactics there: taking back on e4 allows ...d5, forking bishop and knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3.name: Vienna Game: Mieses Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3.background: Vasily Smyslov played it on a few occasions, most notably in a win over Lev Polugaevsky in the 1961 USSR Championship. The best-known example of the fianchetto plan is Jacques Mieses's brilliancy-prize game against Eugene Znosko-Borovsky at Ostend 1907.
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3.strategy: A quiet fianchetto: White prepares to put the king's bishop on the long diagonal, where it supports e4 and bears on the centre, instead of going for the sharp f-pawn break. White gives up early initiative for a solid, flexible set-up and a long game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.a3.name: Vienna Game: Mengarini Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.a3.background: Sometimes called Mengarini's Opening, although Ariel Mengarini actually advocated the move order 1.e4 e5 2.a3, after which 2...Nf6 3.Nc3 transposes; it was Hugh Myers who inserted 2.Nc3 Nf6 before pushing the a-pawn.
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.a3.strategy: A waiting move: it stops ...Bb4 from attacking the c3 knight, but does nothing for the centre or for an attack. White spends a tempo on a flank pawn for a quiet, solid game, and Black can simply develop and equalise.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5.name: Vienna Game: Vienna Gambit, Main Line
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5.strategy: The right counter: instead of grabbing the pawn, Black attacks the e4 pawn a second time and contests the centre. If White captures on e5, the knight takes on e4 with an active piece. Black commits to a sharp, open game in which White's open king diagonal is a target.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d6.strategy: A modest reply that holds the e5 pawn and keeps the centre closed instead of striking back at once. It is sound but passive: White develops freely and chooses when to take on e5, while Black has no active plan of its own.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 exf4.strategy: Grabs the pawn but cannot keep it comfortably: the e-pawn advances with a gain of time, and the attacked knight has no safe square but home, since the queen covers g4 and h5. White gains space and a tempo and can go after the f4 pawn at leisure.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn and attacks the knight with the new e5 pawn, leaving White a pawn up for the moment with the f-file open. Black can restore the balance at once, so White's compensation is activity: open lines and attacking chances, at the cost of a loosened king.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.d3.name: Vienna Game: Vienna Gambit, Steinitz Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.d3.strategy: Shores up e4 with a pawn but gives up the attack on e5. Solid and passive: Black has easy ways to break it down, by exchanging on f4 or by chasing the c3 knight with a pawn, and takes the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.exd5.strategy: Takes a pawn but loosens White's own centre: d5 is attacked twice and defended only by the c3 knight, and the f4 pawn is left without support. Black chooses how to strike back and keeps the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.exd5 e4.strategy: Counters with a pawn thrust that keeps the d5 pawn under fire and cramps White, since the e4 pawn takes d3 and f3 away from White's pieces. Black stays a pawn down for the moment in return for space and the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.exd5 Nxd5.strategy: Wins the pawn back at once with a centralised knight that hits both the c3 knight and the f4 pawn. Material is level and the game is open; if White takes on e5, Black exchanges on c3 and the check on h4 costs White a rook or the right to castle.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.exd5 exf4.strategy: Takes the f-pawn instead of recapturing on d5, so material stays level and ...Nxd5 is still in hand. The cost is time: White develops freely while Black must still hold or return the f4 pawn, so Black spends the next moves defending rather than attacking. Playable, but less direct.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4.strategy: Regains the pawn at once with a centralised knight that hits the c3 knight and is backed by the d5 pawn. Material is level again, so the fight is about open lines: White's f-file and attacking chances against Black's solid centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nfd7.strategy: Retreats and gives up the fight for the pawn: Black stays a pawn down against a cramping e5 pawn, and the knight on d7 blocks the c8 bishop. White has a free hand in the centre and Black has nothing to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Ng4.strategy: Attacks the e5 pawn, but the knight is offside and White simply defends the pawn with a developing move. Black has spent time on a piece that has no follow-up and is still a pawn down.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..strategy: The traditional developing move: it defends the e5 pawn that cramps Black and prepares to castle. White gets open lines and attacking chances, but Black can usually hold the balance with correct play, so it is a fight for the initiative with material level.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..name: Vienna Game: Vienna Gambit, Paulsen Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..background: It is quite common in practice and has been advocated by Ben Finegold.
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..strategy: Brings the queen out at once to the open f-file, where it hits f7 and adds a second attacker to the knight on e4. It plays for quick pressure rather than a calm build-up, leaving the king in the centre and the queen exposed early.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..name: Vienna Game: Vienna Gambit, Modern Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..strategy: Chases the centralised knight with a pawn and opens the c1 bishop's diagonal and the queen's path. It asks Black to commit the knight at once, and a careless reply, such as a hasty queen check, runs into a known trap.

Checks along the open diagonal but walks into a known trap: g3 blocks with a pawn that attacks the queen while the knight on e4 is attacked as well, so both of Black's pieces are under fire. Black gains nothing and has to be precise to avoid trouble.

The knight has no good retreat from the d3 pawn, so Black exchanges it for the c3 knight. If White recaptures with the b-pawn the queenside pawns are doubled; material stays level, and White's open f-file and e5 pawn balance that against Black's solid d5 pawn.

Pins the c3 knight to the king, hoping to keep the e4 knight safe by tactics, but the pawn simply takes it. After dxe4 dxe4 Black has given a whole knight for a pawn and has only the pin and some development to show for it.

Answers the check with a pawn that blocks the diagonal and attacks the queen. If Black grabs it with the knight, Nf3 hits the queen with tempo and, once it steps aside, Nxd5 threatens Nxc7+, forking king and rook.
Steps the king up instead of blocking, and walks into mate: 6...Qf2 is checkmate, the knight on e4 guarding the queen and the king without a flight square.

The knight escapes the d3 pawn by taking a pawn, and now attacks the h1 rook. Black is a pawn up, but White's lead in development gives the better game, and Black must not grab the rook on h1 later, since Nxc7+ forks king and rook.

Counterattacks the white queen. If White takes on h4, Black takes the queen on d1 and the material stays level; but White can recapture on c3 first, and then Black's queen, still attacked, has to lose a tempo to retreat.
Retreats the queen but leaves the e4 knight attacked twice and defended once: White takes it with the d-pawn and, after the recapture, wins a piece for a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..name: Vienna Game: Vienna Gambit, Breyer Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..strategy: The most natural reply: Black develops and prepares to castle, leaving the knight on e4 where it stands, backed by the d5 pawn. Black accepts that White gets open lines and attacking chances, and relies on the solid centre to hold the balance.

Pins the f3 knight to the queen and aims to remove the defender of e5. White can break the pin with tempo by bringing the queen to attack the knight on e4, so the bishop gains little time for its sortie.

Develops with an immediate attack on the e5 pawn while the e4 knight stays put. White has to defend or counterattack, so Black makes the first threats; the price is that White's pieces come into play quickly too and Black's king stays in the centre for now.

Develops on the open diagonal and eyes f2, where a check can force White's king to give up castling. It is a sharper set-up than quiet development, but the d-pawn can challenge the bishop with tempo, and Black has to keep the e4 knight supported.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..name: Vienna Game: Vienna Gambit, Kaufmann Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..strategy: Steps out of the pin and adds a second attacker to the knight on e4, which only the d5 pawn defends. Black has to resolve the tension in the centre at once, while White's e5 pawn keeps cramping Black's position.

Shields the queen by putting the bishop between knight and queen, so the knight is no longer pinned. Black can still trade on f3, and White recaptures with the bishop and keeps the bishop pair, but the move does nothing about the e4 knight and blocks the e2 square for the queen.

Hits the e4 knight with a pawn and opens the c1 bishop, but does not break the pin, so Black first trades on f3 and then on c3. White ends with the bishop pair, but also with doubled c-pawns and an e5 pawn that has no pawn behind it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..name: Vienna Game: Vienna Gambit, Bardeleben Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..background: One of the three usual replies to 5.Qf3, alongside 5...Nxc3 and 5...Nc6.
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..strategy: Backs the knight on e4 with a second pawn and shuts the f-file, so the queen no longer eyes f7. The cost is the e8-h5 diagonal: the king's cover is thinner and White's queen can check there. Black keeps the strong centre but takes on king-safety risk.

The most direct reply: the knight develops with an attack on e5 and leaves the e4 knight in place, though it is attacked twice and held only by the d5 pawn. Black relies on quick piece play against the white queen that came out early; White's e5 pawn is a target.

Trades the strong e4 knight for the c3 knight, breaking up White's queenside pawns if White recaptures with the b-pawn. It gives up the outpost for a simpler game; Black has to watch the open f-file, where the queen eyes f7.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..name: Vienna Game: Heyde Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.f4 d5 4.fxe5 Nxe4 5..strategy: Supports the e5 pawn with a pawn and opens the c1 bishop, building a broad centre that keeps Black's pieces cramped. Black's knight on e4 is held by two pawns, so the fight is whether White's centre or Black's outpost lasts.

Hits the e4 knight with a pawn and opens the c1 bishop, so Black usually trades it for the c3 knight, wrecking White's queenside pawns after bxc3. The cost is that the e5 pawn has no pawn behind it, and ...Nc6 attacks it at once.

Takes en passant at once, trading White's cramping e5 pawn for Black's f-pawn. Black recaptures and the game is open and level, but White has given up the space advantage that made the gambit worthwhile.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 d5.strategy: Hits the centre at once: with the bishop not yet on g2, e4 is attacked by the d-pawn and the knight and defended only by the c3 knight, so White must resolve the tension. Black gets a sound structure and a fair game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 Bc5.strategy: A quieter developing move: the bishop eyes f2 and Black keeps the central strike in hand. It is slower and less direct, but flexible, and it leaves White to decide whether to play for the centre or keep the game closed.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops the queen's knight and protects e5, keeping the centre pawn solid while the d-pawn and bishop stay flexible. A quiet, flexible reply: Black waits to see whether White plays for the centre or sticks to the fianchetto.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 Bc5 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop supports e4 and prepares castling, sitting behind the e4 pawn until the centre opens. White keeps a solid, flexible set-up and a slow game of manoeuvring rather than a fight for immediate gains.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 Bc5 4.Nge2.strategy: Develops the king's knight to e2, where it covers the c3 knight and the g3 pawn and keeps the long diagonal clear for the bishop that is to come to g2. It also leaves the f-pawn free to advance later.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 Bc5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops with an attack on the e5 pawn, which Black has to defend. The knight stands on the diagonal of the bishop that is to go to g2, but the e4 pawn is poisoned: after ...Nxe4 Nxe4 d5 the knight takes the bishop on c5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 Bc5 4.Bg2 Nc6.strategy: Develops the last knight and defends e5, finishing a compact set-up in which Black has no clear weaknesses. Neither side has committed to a pawn structure, so the game is balanced and flexible, a test of who finds the better plan.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 Bc5 4.Bg2 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and opens the c8 bishop, giving the centre a firm base. Black keeps the bishop on c5 aimed at f2 and the game compact and flexible, a little slower than developing the knight but just as solid.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 Bc5 4.Bg2 O-O.strategy: Castles at once, which is safe but leaves the e5 pawn unprotected for now, so White can attack it with a developing move and Black has to spend the next moves defending it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 d5 4.exd5.strategy: Resolves the tension in White's favour: the e-pawn takes Black's central pawn. If Black recaptures with the knight, it stands on d5 where the c3 knight and the coming bishop on g2 can challenge it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 d5 4.Nxd5.strategy: Trades knights and opens the centre, but gives up the tension without a gain: after the recapture with the queen, Black's centralised queen and the e5 pawn give Black the bigger share of the centre. A harmless simplification that hands Black an easy game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 d5 4.Bg2.strategy: Develops the bishop and defends e4 a second time, so that ...dxe4 can be met by Nxe4 and the bishop recaptures. White gets a solid, slightly passive set-up and leaves Black to decide whether to release the tension.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 d5 4.exd5 c6.name: Vienna Game: Mieses Variation, Erben Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 d5 4.exd5 c6.strategy: A gambit: instead of recapturing, Black lets White take a second pawn to open lines for the pieces. White can simply accept and finish development, and Black is a pawn down with no forced gain to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 d5 4.exd5 Nxd5.strategy: Recaptures the pawn at once and brings the knight to the centre, where it hits the c3 knight. Material is level; White's knight and the coming bishop on g2 can challenge the d5 knight, but Black gets a sound structure and a fair game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 d5 4.exd5 e4.strategy: Pushes the e-pawn to cramp White, since the e4 pawn takes d3 and f3 from White's pieces, and keeps ...Nxd5 ready. Black stays a pawn down for the moment and has to justify it with space and quick play, so recapturing at once is simpler.

1.e4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.g3 d5 4.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Hangs the queen: Nxd5 wins it for a knight, and Black has no way to get the material back.
